label: Garry Nolan
narrative: Nolan is the most credentialed working scientist to put his name to UAP materials analysis, and the reason the subject now has a peer-reviewed footprint at all. He has held the Harris endowed chair in pathology at Stanford since 2011, founded Rigel, Nodality, BINA Technology (sold to Roche for $107m) and Akoya Biosciences, and co-developed CODEX and multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) with Michael Angelo and Sean Bendall - the same MIBI instrument he then turned on alleged UAP debris. His entry into the field was not voluntary in the ordinary sense: he told KQED in June 2021 that he was approached by 'some people representing the government and an aerospace corporation to help them understand the medical harm that had come to some individuals, related to supposed interactions with an anomalous craft', because 'they were interested in the kinds of blood analysis that my lab can do'. That is the crux for this board - an unnamed government element and an unnamed aerospace corporation walking human casualty material into a Stanford pathology laboratory. In January 2022 he published, with Jacques Vallee, Sizun Jiang and former NASA Ames engineer Larry Lemke, the first serious peer-reviewed instrumental study of alleged UAP material in Progress in Aerospace Sciences, applying SIMS and MIBI at 200 nm lateral resolution to the 1977 Council Bluffs, Iowa molten-metal mass. The finding is genuinely awkward for both camps: no anomalous isotope ratios, but incomplete mixing of the constituent metals indicating an industrial process of unknown origin, with meteoritic, satellite, aircraft, dumping and thermite explanations each argued away. In May 2023 at the SALT iConnections conference he said governments have retrieved artefacts from extraterrestrial craft and put the probability of long-term extraterrestrial visitation at '100 percent'. He co-founded The Sol Foundation with Peter Skafish on 15 August 2023, and in June 2026 was named to the White House-requested UAP Science Advisory Council.
